text: Three husbands, one wife, one house on hard ground in the Brazilian northeast, and the picture plays it as domestic routine rather than scandal. Andrucha Waddington built it from a true story and kept it to 106 minutes, long enough to show the household's economy: who fetches water, who works the field, who sleeps where. The comedy comes from arithmetic. Karlovy Vary gave it the Crystal Globe and named its lead the festival's best actress, and Brazil sent it forward as its submission to the Academy Awards. What holds the center is labor. The land is poor, the days are long, and the arrangement runs on divided work as much as on affection, which is why a setup built for farce keeps declining to become one.

A truck loaded with timber leaves Paraguay for Buenos Aires with three people in the cab, one of them five months old. Rubén did not agree to the baby, and no one asked him. His employer arranged the passenger, Jacinta, and her daughter Anahí arrives as a fact he has to drive with. Pablo Giorgelli gives the situation 85 minutes and almost nothing else: a windshield, a road, two adults with no reason to speak and many hours in which to do it. The Caméra d'Or and the Silver Condor for best film followed. The romance in the genre line is not a plot but a possibility that accumulates or does not, kilometre by kilometre, and the film trusts small evidence to carry it: who holds the child, who pays for lunch, who looks over first.

The mountain is sacred to the people living beneath it and a prize to the British expedition marching toward it. Feng Xiaoning keeps that collision waiting for a long stretch and gives the time to something smaller: a Chinese girl who has fled a sacrifice, the Tibetan herdsman who takes her in, a proud princess, and the daily etiquette the newcomer keeps getting wrong. Manners are the subject before rifles are. Then the expedition reaches the edge of the sacred ground, private grievance has to be set down, and a militia forms out of people who were quarreling an hour earlier. Made in 1997 and given the Huabiao and the Hundred Flowers for best picture, the film works at the scale of landscape: high altitude, wide weather, small parties of humans crossing it.

A Jesuit walks upriver into the South American interior to build a mission, and the man who used to sell its people into slavery follows him there. What Roland Joffé is after across 125 minutes is not conversion but the moment a treaty signed in Europe reaches a clearing in the forest: Spain hands the colony to Portugal, and everything built on the ground becomes negotiable. The picture took the Palme d'Or and a place on the National Board of Review's top ten, and the Academy honored its cinematography, which argues rather than decorates, since the scale of the country is what makes the mission both possible and impossible to defend. Two men hold the moral question between them, one who came to save the people there and one who came to take them, and neither position is allowed to be simply right.

In 1979 a television reporter assigned a soft feature on energy sources is standing in a viewing gallery when the needles move and the men below her stop talking. Kimberly Wells leaves with footage and no way to air it, which is where James Bridges puts his thriller: not in the reactor but in the offices where a story is softened, delayed, or reassigned. The tension is procedural. Who signs off, who is available for comment, whose word counts as evidence. The Writers Guild gave it their award for original screenplay and the Academy recognized both lead performances, which suits a film that runs on people arguing in rooms for 122 minutes. Its subject is the gap between what a technician knows, what a network will broadcast, and what a company will concede.

A man is dead in 1947 and the suspects are all soldiers, out of the army a matter of days and still moving in a pack. Which one did it is the surface question; Edward Dmytryk is after the other one, why, and motive turns out to be the more damaging investigation. The film runs 86 minutes and spends most of them in rooms, questioning, waiting, drinking, filling the long civilian evenings these men have no idea what to do with. Compression is the method: with no time for procedure, everything has to come out of the way people talk when they are tired and frightened. It carries a Palme d'Or and a place on the National Board of Review's top ten. Nothing about the case is complicated except the men in it.

The rule is simple, no violence ever, and the household keeps discovering how much of ordinary life it covers. William Wyler gives a Quaker family in Indiana in 1862 the better part of 137 minutes, and most of that time goes to small breaches rather than large ones: vanity, temper, the wish to win at something, the pleasures a plain life is not supposed to want. By the time Southern troops move through the county, the doctrine has been negotiated over trivia for two hours, and the large question lands on individuals rather than on the family as a body. That is the harder arrangement and the more interesting one. It took the Palme d'Or and a place on the National Board of Review's top ten. Almost everything in it is domestic, and almost nothing is settled in advance.

Pontus has not eaten in some time and has not stopped writing, and Christiania in 1890 has no use for either fact. He wants love and he wants print, and hunger keeps rewriting both wants into something stranger: elation in one hour, contempt for everyone in the next, a grip on the actual world that loosens by the day. Henning Carlsen gives this 112 minutes and stays with the man rather than the city, which makes the film a performance problem before it is anything else. The lead took a best actor prize, the Bodil went to it as the year's best Danish film, and Denmark sent it forward as its submission to the Academy Awards. Pride is the plot. Whatever dignity the character keeps, he pays for in food, and the film counts the price item by item.

The party heading for the Swiss border has no common language, which is a practical problem long before it is a theme. Two escaped prisoners of war, one American and one British, come off a train in wartime Italy and end up leading a mixed group of refugees at the underground's request, less because they know the route than because someone has to count heads. Switzerland made the film in 1945, in German, about the frontier at its own back, and the 113 minutes give the terrain the weight another war picture would hand an enemy: distance, altitude, weather, the pace of the slowest walker. It was named to the National Board of Review's top ten and given a Golden Globe in a category of the period, for a film promoting international understanding. Nothing here turns on heroism. It turns on whether the group keeps moving together.

A doctor with a good name in a small Romanian city starts making phone calls, and every one of them is a favor that will have to be returned. His daughter was attacked days before the examinations that decide whether she takes up her place in the UK, and the injury puts the result in doubt. Cristian Mungiu builds 128 minutes out of that arithmetic: a word with the right official, a signature moved forward, a debt accepted on both sides, and not one of the transactions looks monstrous on its own. The European Film Awards named him best director and best screenwriter, and audiences there voted it the year's European film. What the father calls protection is also instruction, since he is showing his daughter in detail how the system he wants her to escape actually operates.

A hotel goes on running, rooms assigned, liquor accounted for, staff on rota, while the killing outside it takes more than a million lives. Paul Rusesabagina shelters over a thousand people inside a business, and the film is most precise when it treats survival as management: what can be traded, who can be flattered, how long a favor holds before it has to be bought again. Terry George made it in 2004, close enough to the events that the fact in its premise still stung, a genocide the rest of the world mostly did not watch. It took a place on the National Board of Review's top ten and a People's Choice award, and the Academy recognized its lead performance, a supporting performance and its screenplay. Most of the 122 minutes stay indoors, which is a moral decision as much as a structural one.

Thirty thousand jobs left Flint, Michigan, and a man with a camera decided the appropriate response was to request a meeting. Michael Moore wants Roger Smith, the chief executive of General Motors, to come to Flint and look at what closing the plant did, and the pursuit gives a film about deindustrialization the shape of a comedy about access: lobbies, receptionists, the floors an appointment is required to reach. Across 91 minutes it keeps cutting back to the town, where the same arithmetic is not funny at all. The joke and the reporting are one gesture. It sits in the National Film Registry. The argument under the running joke has less to do with one executive than with how much distance a corporation can put between a decision and the street where it lands.

Gerry Conlon was a small-time thief in Belfast, and that was the whole of his record when England charged him with mass murder. He is convicted of an IRA bombing in London he had nothing to do with, and his father is convicted alongside him, which is where Jim Sheridan finds the film he actually wants: two men who could barely share a room and now share a sentence. Fifteen years is the figure the picture has to make felt. It does that domestically, in the slower half of the story, where a son learns what his father is made of at the worst possible time. It took the Golden Bear and a place on the National Board of Review's top ten, and the Academy recognized its lead performance, its direction and its editing. At 133 minutes it is patient with the prison and impatient with everything that filled it.

Seventy-four minutes, and a surprising number of them belong to the mice. The 1950 Cinderella spends far more time on a house in motion, chores repeated until they turn into rhythm, small animals running operations behind the walls, than on anything at the palace, and that economy is why it still moves. Sound carries much of the load: the Academy gave it awards for its score and its sound, which for a musical drawn frame by frame amounts to saying the picture was built at the mixing desk as much as at the drawing board. It holds a Golden Bear and a place in the National Film Registry. Clyde Geronimi is working in a register where cruelty is domestic and daily rather than monstrous, and where housework is filmed as work.
